routes: The Roman conquest of Gaul (58–51 BCE) brings Gallo-Roman religion
The Roman conquest of southern Britain (43)
marks: The Warrior of Hirschlanden, a stone figure of the 6th century BCE, is among the earliest Celtic monumental sculptures.
The 5th-century BCE stone figure known as the “Glauberg Prince” comes from this site in Germany.
A carved stone head, probably of the 2nd century BCE, was found here in Bohemia.
Offerings, mostly of battle gear, were thrown into this lake on Anglesey in the late 1st century BCE or early 1st century CE.
The Pillar of the Boatmen, with many figures of gods, is dated by its dedication to the emperor Tiberius (r. from 14 CE).
The Coligny calendar, the oldest attested Celtic calendar, dates to the 2nd century.
notes: The Celtic peoples of Iron Age Europe worship many gods in groves, at springs and in timber shrines; the earliest stone figures, from southern Germany, date to the 6th and 5th centuries BCE.
Celtic coins, struck from the late 4th century BCE, carry heads and horses that may have had religious meaning; weapons are offered in rivers, lakes and bogs.
Rome conquers Gaul (58–51 BCE); Julius Caesar describes the druids and names the Gaulish gods after Roman ones.
Under Augustus and Tiberius the druidic hierarchies are suppressed, and Celtic and Roman gods merge in a Gallo-Roman religion; Rome conquers southern Britain in 43.
The Coligny calendar, the oldest attested Celtic calendar, is made in Roman Gaul in the 2nd century.
The Gauls begin gradually to convert to Christianity, from the 3rd century onward.
Roman rule in Britain ends (c. 410) and Anglo-Saxon paganism replaces Celtic paganism over much of England; the Celtic peoples of Britain and Ireland convert gradually from the 5th century.
By the early 7th century the Irish church has relegated the druids to irrelevancy, while the filid keep much of their pre-Christian learning.
